title: 392. You're Really Good At Doing It Wrong
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter
summary: The Best Leadership Newsletter opens with the author's wrecked knee: decades of running with an undiagnosed foot flare meant every step reinforced a bad movement pattern until something broke. From there the piece argues that experience is not expertise, citing a 2005 Harvard Medical School review in which more than half the studies found that doctors with more years in practice gave worse quality of care. It also corrects the 10,000-hour rule, noting that Anders Ericsson's point was how you practice, not how long, and concludes that "practice makes permanent" rather than perfect. Applied to leadership, every avoided hard conversation, phone check in a meeting, or unaddressed missed commitment is a rep of a bad habit. The author warns that the warning signs, such as a quieter team or departing good employees, are routinely explained away, and ends by asking the reader what they actually practiced today.
points: Experience only makes you better at whatever you were actually practicing, so twenty years of leading can be one year of mistakes repeated twenty times.
The 10,000-hour rule misreads Ericsson, whose work stressed the quality and method of practice over the number of hours.
Everyday avoidance, distraction and tolerated broken commitments are reps, and they compound into a leadership style without ever feeling like practice.
Warning signs like a quieter team, challenges to your ideas drying up, or good people leaving are easy to rationalize as bad luck or a rough quarter.
The diagnostic question for any leader is not what they meant to practice but what they did repeatedly without thinking today.
quotes: Most people believe that if you do something enough times, you’ll get great at it. Log enough hours and eventually you’ll be a master.
More than half of the studies found that the more years a doctor practiced, the worse their quality of care.
Think of it as the difference between 20 years of experience, and one year of experience that you’ve repeated 20 times.
The hours were never the point of his work. What matters most is not the amount of time you practice, but how you do it.
Every time you avoid a hard conversation, you’re practicing avoidance.
Every time you let someone miss a commitment without addressing it, you’re practicing a lack of accountability.
The problem isn’t that you don’t see the consequences. It’s that you’ve gotten really good at explaining them away.
Not what you meant to practice. What you actually did. Over and over. Without thinking about it.
